rooms.about: This year we read chapter books, myths and nonfiction, learn to find main ideas and themes, build vocabulary, and write stories, opinions and short reports with strong paragraphs.

learn: Strong readers think while they read. They ask questions, make pictures in their minds and check that the words make sense.
If something does not make sense, stop and reread. Try reading the sentence aloud or looking at the pictures.
Fluent readers read smoothly, at a good pace and with expression. Their voice goes up for questions and gets excited at exclamation marks.
Reading for about 20 minutes a day helps you learn hundreds of new words each year.
units.try: Choose a page from a chapter book. Read it aloud twice. The second time, add expression, as if you were reading to a younger child. Then ask yourself two questions about the page and answer them.
check: What should you do if a sentence does not make sense?

learn: Many words have parts. The base word is the main part. A prefix is added to the beginning. A suffix is added to the end.
Common prefixes: un means not (unhappy), re means again (redo), pre means before (preview), dis means not or opposite (disagree).
Common suffixes: ful means full of (hopeful), less means without (fearless), er can mean a person who (teacher), ly often tells how (quickly).
Context clues are hints in nearby words. In The arid desert had no rain for months, the clue no rain tells you arid means very dry.
units.try: Break these words into parts and tell what each means: unkind, replay, careless, helpful. For example, unkind = un (not) + kind, so it means not kind.
check: What does the prefix re mean?

learn: Characters have traits. A trait describes what someone is like inside, such as brave, honest, selfish or curious.
Authors show traits through what characters say, do and think. If a girl shares her lunch with a new student, she is showing kindness.
Characters' actions cause events in the plot. One choice can lead to a chain of events.
Readers use evidence, or proof from the text, to support what they say about a character.
units.try: Think of a main character from a book you read. Name one trait. Then find two things the character did or said that prove it, and write them as evidence.
check: What a character is like inside

learn: Folktales are old stories passed down by telling them aloud. Many cultures have their own.
A fable is a short story that teaches a lesson, often with animals. A myth explains something in nature, like why the seasons change, and often has gods or heroes.
The central message, or theme, is the big idea the story teaches, such as honesty matters or work together.
Many cultures tell similar stories. There are Cinderella-like tales from China, Egypt and Europe, each with different details.
units.try: Retell a fable or folktale you know in five sentences: beginning, two middle events, problem solved, and lesson. Then say the central message in one short sentence.
check: What does a myth often explain?
What is the theme of a story?

learn: The main idea is what a paragraph or article is mostly about. Key details support or explain the main idea.
The main idea is often in the first or last sentence, but not always. Ask: What do all the sentences have in common?
Example: Bats help people. They eat many insects. They spread seeds. They pollinate plants. The main idea is that bats help people; the other sentences are details.
A summary tells the main idea and the most important details in your own words. It is short and leaves out small details.
units.try: Read a short nonfiction article. Write the main idea in one sentence. Then list three key details that support it. Use your own words.
check: What should a summary leave out?

learn: Text features help you find information. They include headings, maps, diagrams, timelines, bold words, captions, an index and a glossary.
An index is an alphabetical list at the back that shows which pages talk about a topic.
Authors organize information in structures. Sequence tells steps in order. Compare and contrast tells how things are alike and different. Cause and effect tells why something happened.
Signal words help: first and then show sequence; but and both show comparing; because and so show cause and effect.
units.try: Find a nonfiction book. Use the index to find a page about one topic. Then read that page and decide if it uses sequence, compare and contrast, or cause and effect.
check: At the back of a book
Which signal word shows cause and effect?

learn: Nouns name things. Pronouns take their place: he, she, it, they, we. Verbs show action or being. Adjectives describe nouns. Adverbs describe verbs, often telling how, when or where: slowly, yesterday, outside.
Verb tenses show time. Past: I walked. Present: I walk. Future: I will walk. Some verbs are irregular: go, went; eat, ate; see, saw.
Subjects and verbs must agree. One dog barks. Two dogs bark.
Comparative adjectives compare two things: taller. Superlatives compare three or more: tallest. For long words use more and most: more careful, most careful.
units.try: Write one sentence about yesterday, one about today and one about tomorrow, using the verb play. Then underline one adverb you used.
check: What is the past tense of go?

learn: A paragraph is a group of sentences about one main idea.
The topic sentence tells the main idea. Detail sentences support it. A closing sentence wraps it up.
Linking words connect ideas: also, another, for example, because, therefore, since.
Use quotation marks around the exact words someone says. Put a comma before the quote: Mom said, “Time for dinner.”
units.try: Write a paragraph about your favorite animal. Start with a topic sentence. Add three detail sentences using the words also and for example. End with a closing sentence.
check: What does a topic sentence do?

learn: A narrative tells a story with characters, a setting and a plot. Hook the reader with an interesting beginning, like a sound, a question or action.
Use dialogue, or characters talking, to bring the story to life. Start a new paragraph each time a new person speaks.
Show, don't just tell. Instead of She was nervous, write Her hands shook as she opened the door.
Build to a problem and give a clear ending that solves it.
units.try: Write a short story about finding a mysterious box. Start with a hook. Include at least two lines of dialogue in quotation marks. Show one feeling through actions.
check: Which sentence shows instead of tells?
His knees shook as he stepped on stage.

learn: Opinion writing states what you think and supports it with reasons. Each reason needs facts or examples.
Use a clear structure: introduce your opinion, give at least two reasons with linking words, and end with a conclusion.
A research report shares facts about a topic. Gather information from books and trusted sources. Take notes in your own words.
Sort your notes into categories, like habitat, food and life cycle. Each category becomes a paragraph.
units.try: Write an opinion piece: Should students have homework? Give your opinion, two reasons with examples, and a conclusion. Use the words because and for example.
check: How should you take research notes?

rooms.about: This year we learn to multiply and divide within 100, round and add or subtract within 1,000, understand fractions, and measure time, mass, volume, area and perimeter.

learn: Multiplication is a fast way to add equal groups. 4 groups of 3 is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12. We write 4 × 3 = 12.
The numbers we multiply are factors. The answer is the product. In 4 × 3 = 12, the factors are 4 and 3 and the product is 12.
An array is objects in equal rows and columns. An array with 4 rows of 3 shows 4 × 3.
Order does not change the product: 4 × 3 = 3 × 4. This is the commutative property.
units.try: There are 5 bags with 6 apples in each. How many apples? Step 1: This is 5 equal groups of 6. Step 2: Write 5 × 6. Step 3: Skip count by 6 five times: 6, 12, 18, 24, 30. There are 30 apples.

learn: Learn the easy facts first. Any number × 0 = 0. Any number × 1 = that number. × 2 is doubling. × 5 products end in 0 or 5. × 10 adds a zero: 7 × 10 = 70.
Use a fact you know to find one you don't. To find 6 × 7, think 5 × 7 = 35, plus one more 7 = 42.
The distributive property lets you split a factor. 8 × 7 = 8 × 5 + 8 × 2 = 40 + 16 = 56.
The associative property lets you group factors any way: (2 × 3) × 4 = 2 × (3 × 4) = 24.
units.try: Find 9 × 6 by splitting. Step 1: Think of 9 × 6 as 10 × 6 minus 1 × 6. Step 2: 10 × 6 = 60. Step 3: 60 − 6 = 54. So 9 × 6 = 54.

learn: Division splits a number into equal groups. 12 ÷ 3 = 4 means 12 shared into 3 equal groups gives 4 in each group.
Division can also ask how many groups. 12 ÷ 3 can mean: how many groups of 3 are in 12? The answer is 4 groups.
The number being divided is the dividend. The number you divide by is the divisor. The answer is the quotient.
You cannot divide by 0. Any number divided by 1 is itself. Any number (not 0) divided by itself is 1.
units.try: 24 stickers are shared equally by 4 friends. How many does each get? Step 1: Write 24 ÷ 4. Step 2: Think: 4 × ? = 24. Step 3: 4 × 6 = 24, so each friend gets 6 stickers.
check: In 18 ÷ 3 = 6, which number is the quotient?

learn: Multiplication and division are related. They form fact families. For 3, 7 and 21: 3 × 7 = 21, 7 × 3 = 21, 21 ÷ 3 = 7, 21 ÷ 7 = 3.
Use multiplication to solve division. To find 56 ÷ 8, ask 8 × what = 56? Since 8 × 7 = 56, the answer is 7.
A letter or box can stand for an unknown number. In 6 × n = 42, n = 7.
By the end of grade 3, you should know all products of two one-digit numbers from memory.
units.try: Solve 4 × □ = 36. Step 1: Ask which number times 4 makes 36. Step 2: Count by 4s: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 28, 32, 36. Step 3: That is 9 fours, so □ = 9.
check: Which fact is in the same family as 5 × 8 = 40?

learn: Rounding gives a number that is close and easy to work with. To round to the nearest ten, look at the ones digit. If it is 5 or more, round up. If it is less than 5, round down.
Examples: 47 rounds to 50. 342 rounds to 340 (nearest ten) and 300 (nearest hundred). 650 rounds to 700 (nearest hundred).
Add and subtract within 1,000 using place value. Line up hundreds, tens and ones. Regroup when needed.
Estimate first to check if your answer is reasonable. 398 + 207 is about 400 + 200 = 600.
units.try: Solve 503 − 278. Step 1: You cannot take 8 from 3, and there are 0 tens, so trade 1 hundred for 10 tens: 4 hundreds, 10 tens, 3 ones. Step 2: Trade 1 ten for 10 ones: 4 hundreds, 9 tens, 13 ones. Step 3: 13 − 8 = 5, 9 − 7 = 2, 4 − 2 = 2. The answer is 225.
check: What is 463 rounded to the nearest hundred?

learn: Some word problems take two steps. Read carefully and decide what to do first.
Example: Sam has 3 packs of 8 cards. He gives away 5. How many are left? Step 1: 3 × 8 = 24. Step 2: 24 − 5 = 19.
Use a letter for the unknown and check whether your answer is reasonable.
Look for patterns. In the multiplication table, any number times an even number gives an even product. The products of 5 always end in 0 or 5.
units.try: A class of 28 students splits into teams of 4. Each team gets 3 balls. How many balls are needed? Step 1: 28 ÷ 4 = 7 teams. Step 2: 7 × 3 = 21 balls.
check: Maria has 4 boxes of 6 crayons and buys 10 more. How many now?

learn: A fraction names part of a whole that is split into equal parts. The bottom number, the denominator, tells how many equal parts make the whole. The top number, the numerator, tells how many parts we have.
In ¾, the whole is split into 4 equal parts and we have 3 of them.
Fractions are numbers and can go on a number line. To show ⅓, split the space from 0 to 1 into 3 equal parts. The first mark is ⅓.
When the numerator equals the denominator, the fraction is one whole: 4/4 = 1. Whole numbers can be fractions too: 3 = 3/1.
units.try: Draw a number line from 0 to 1. Split it into 4 equal parts. Label the marks 1/4, 2/4, 3/4 and 4/4. Where is 4/4? It is at 1.
check: In 2/5, what does the 5 tell you?

learn: Equivalent fractions name the same amount. 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6. On number lines of the same length, they land on the same point.
With the same denominator, compare numerators. 3/8 > 2/8, because 3 pieces is more than 2 pieces of the same size.
With the same numerator, compare denominators. 1/3 > 1/6, because thirds are bigger pieces than sixths. More equal parts means smaller pieces.
Only compare fractions of the same size whole. Half a large pizza is more than half a small one.
units.try: Compare 2/3 and 2/5. Step 1: The numerators are the same. Step 2: Thirds are bigger pieces than fifths. Step 3: So 2/3 > 2/5.

learn: Tell time to the nearest minute. Find elapsed time by counting on: from 2:45 p.m. to 3:20 p.m. is 15 minutes to 3:00 plus 20 minutes, or 35 minutes.
Liquid volume is measured in liters (L). Mass is measured in grams (g) and kilograms (kg). 1 kilogram = 1,000 grams. A paper clip is about 1 gram.
Scaled bar graphs and picture graphs can use one symbol for many. If one star = 5 votes, 3 stars mean 15 votes.
A line plot shows measurements on a number line, with an X for each one. It can use halves and fourths of an inch.
units.try: A movie starts at 4:15 p.m. and ends at 5:50 p.m. How long is it? Step 1: 4:15 to 5:15 is 1 hour. Step 2: 5:15 to 5:50 is 35 minutes. Step 3: The movie is 1 hour 35 minutes.
check: How many grams are in 1 kilogram?
If one picture = 4 books, how many books do 5 pictures show?

learn: Area is the amount of space inside a flat shape. It is measured in square units. For a rectangle, area = length × width. A 4 cm by 3 cm rectangle has area 12 square centimeters.
Perimeter is the distance around a shape. Add all the side lengths. The same 4 by 3 rectangle has perimeter 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 cm.
Shapes with the same area can have different perimeters. A 6 by 1 rectangle and a 3 by 2 rectangle both have area 6, but perimeters 14 and 10.
Quadrilaterals have 4 sides. A rectangle has 4 right angles. A square has 4 right angles and 4 equal sides. A rhombus has 4 equal sides. A square is both a rectangle and a rhombus.
units.try: Find the area and perimeter of a garden 5 m long and 2 m wide. Step 1: Area = 5 × 2 = 10 square meters. Step 2: Perimeter = 5 + 2 + 5 + 2 = 14 meters.
check: What is the area of a 7 by 3 rectangle?
Which shape has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles?

rooms.about: This year we study forces, motion and magnets, the life cycles and traits of living things, fossils and survival, and weather, climate and natural hazards.

learn: A force is a push or a pull. Forces can make things start moving, stop, speed up, slow down or change direction.
Every force has a strength and a direction. A gentle tap is a weak force. A hard kick is a strong force.
Gravity is a force that pulls objects toward Earth. That is why a dropped ball falls down.
Friction is a force that slows things down when surfaces rub together. A ball rolls farther on a smooth floor than on thick carpet.
units.try: Roll a toy car down a ramp made from a book and a board. Measure how far it goes on a smooth floor, then on a towel. Which surface has more friction?
check: Which force pulls objects toward Earth?

learn: When forces on an object are balanced, they cancel out. The object does not change its motion. A book resting on a table has balanced forces: gravity pulls down and the table pushes up.
In tug-of-war, if both teams pull equally hard, the rope does not move. The forces are balanced.
Unbalanced forces change an object's motion. If one team pulls harder, the rope moves toward that team.
The bigger the unbalanced force, the bigger the change in motion.
units.try: Place a small ball on a table. Gently blow on it from one side. It moves: unbalanced force. Now have a partner blow equally from the other side at the same time. What happens?
check: What happens when forces are balanced?
In tug-of-war, the rope moves left. The forces are…

learn: Some motions repeat in a pattern. Scientists can use the pattern to predict what will happen next.
A pendulum is a weight hanging from a string that swings back and forth. A playground swing works like a pendulum.
A shorter pendulum swings faster. A longer one swings slower. The weight of the object matters very little.
Other patterns: a bouncing ball bounces lower each time, and a spinning top slows down and wobbles.
units.try: Tie a washer to a string. Hold the string and let it swing. Count swings in 15 seconds. Now make the string half as long and count again. Which swings more times?
check: They help us predict what happens next

learn: Magnets pull on objects made of iron, nickel or steel. They do not attract wood, plastic, glass or most coins.
Every magnet has a north pole and a south pole. Opposite poles attract, or pull together. Like poles repel, or push apart.
Magnets can work without touching, and even through paper. The force gets weaker as the magnet gets farther away.
Static electricity is another non-touching force. Rub a balloon on your hair and it can pick up small bits of paper or make your hair stand up.
units.try: Test objects around the house with a fridge magnet: a spoon, a paper clip, a crayon, a key, foil. Make a chart of which ones stick. Then rub a balloon on a sweater and hold it near tiny paper bits.
check: What happens when two north poles meet?
Which object will a magnet pull?

learn: All living things have a life cycle. They are born, grow, reproduce and die.
Many insects go through complete metamorphosis with four stages. A butterfly goes from egg, to larva (caterpillar), to pupa (chrysalis), to adult.
A frog changes from egg to tadpole, which lives in water and breathes with gills, then to froglet and adult frog with lungs.
Plants have life cycles too: seed, sprout, adult plant, flower, and new seeds.
units.try: Draw the life cycle of a butterfly as a circle with four stages. Label each one: egg, larva, pupa, adult. Add arrows to show the order.
check: What is the larva stage of a butterfly?

learn: Traits are features of a living thing. Inherited traits are passed from parents to their young, like eye color, the shape of a leaf or the spots on a dog.
Young animals are similar to their parents but not exactly the same. Puppies in one litter can look different.
The environment can also change traits. A plant with little light grows tall and pale. A person who exercises builds stronger muscles.
Learned behaviors are not inherited. Riding a bike or reading is learned.
units.try: Look at family photos. Find one trait you share with a parent or relative, like hair color or dimples. Then name one thing you learned to do that was not inherited.
check: Can the environment change a living thing's traits?
Yes, like a plant growing pale without light

learn: A fossil is the remains or trace of a living thing from long ago, preserved in rock. Bones, shells, footprints and leaf prints can become fossils.
Most fossils form when a living thing is buried in mud or sand that slowly hardens into rock over millions of years.
Fossils tell us about past environments. Fossil fish found on a mountain show that the area was once covered by water.
Some living things that once lived are now extinct, which means none are alive anymore. Dinosaurs, other than birds, went extinct about 66 million years ago.
units.try: Press a shell, leaf or toy into a flat piece of clay or play dough, then remove it. You made a model of a trace fossil. What could a scientist learn from it?
check: Fossil fish on a mountain tell us the area was once…

learn: An adaptation is a trait that helps a living thing survive in its environment.
Camouflage helps animals blend in, like a white arctic fox in snow. Thick blubber keeps whales warm. Cactuses store water in their stems.
Some animals live in groups to survive. Wolves hunt in packs, fish swim in schools and bees share work in a hive.
When an environment changes, some living things survive well, some move away and some die. Within a kind of animal, those with helpful traits are more likely to survive and have young.
units.try: Invent an animal that lives in a very hot desert. Draw it and label three adaptations that help it survive, like how it finds water or stays cool.
check: How do cactuses survive dry places?
They store water in their stems

learn: Weather is what the air is like at a certain time and place: temperature, rain, wind and clouds. It can change hour by hour.
Climate is the usual weather pattern of a place over many years. Deserts have a dry climate. Rainforests have a hot, wet climate.
Scientists measure weather with tools. A thermometer measures temperature. A rain gauge measures rainfall. A wind vane shows wind direction.
Recording weather in tables and graphs helps scientists find patterns and make forecasts, or predictions.
units.try: Keep a weather journal for one week. Each day, record the temperature, clouds and whether it rained. At the end, make a bar graph of the temperatures.
check: The usual weather of a place over many years
What does a rain gauge measure?

learn: A natural hazard is a natural event that can harm people or property, like floods, hurricanes, tornadoes, earthquakes and wildfires.

We cannot stop these events, but we can design ways to reduce harm. Levees and walls hold back flood water. Buildings can be made to sway in earthquakes. Lightning rods guide lightning safely to the ground.
Weather forecasts and warning sirens give people time to get to safety.
Families should have an emergency plan and a kit with water, food, a flashlight and first-aid supplies.
units.try: With your family, make an emergency plan. Choose a safe place in your home for storms and a meeting place outside. List five items for an emergency kit.
check: What does a lightning rod do?
Guides lightning safely to the ground

rooms.about: This year we study communities near and far: how geography shapes them, how they change over time, how local government works, how people earn and spend money, and the many cultures that make up our country.

learn: Geographers study places and how people live in them. Maps are their main tool.
A map scale shows real distance. If 1 inch equals 10 miles, then 3 inches on the map means 30 miles.
Lines of latitude run east and west. Lines of longitude run north and south. The equator is the line of latitude halfway between the North and South Poles.
Intermediate directions are between the main ones: northeast, northwest, southeast and southwest.
units.try: Use a map of your state. Find your town and the state capital. Use the scale to estimate how many miles apart they are, and say which direction the capital is from you.
check: What does a map scale show?
Which direction is between north and east?

learn: Landforms and resources affect where people settle. Many cities grew next to rivers, lakes or coasts because water was needed for drinking, farming and travel.
Natural resources are things from nature people use, like water, trees, soil, fish and minerals.
People adapt to their environment. In cold places, people build warm homes and wear heavy clothes. In hot places, homes may have thick walls or shade.
People also change the environment by building dams, roads and farms. Some changes help, and some cause problems like pollution.
units.try: Look at a map of the United States. Find three big cities. Is each one near water? Write down which river, lake or ocean is close to it.
check: Why did many cities grow near rivers?

learn: Native Americans were the first people to live in North America. They lived here for thousands of years before Europeans arrived.

There were hundreds of nations, each with its own language and way of life. The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) built longhouses and grew corn, beans and squash. Plains nations such as the Lakota followed the buffalo.
Native nations used the resources around them for food, clothing, homes and tools.
Many Native nations still live and thrive today. They keep their languages and traditions and have their own governments.
units.try: Find out which Native nation or nations first lived where you live today. Write three facts about them, such as their homes, foods or language.
check: Who were the first people in North America?
What three crops did the Haudenosaunee grow together?

learn: Communities change over time. A small village may grow into a large city.
New inventions bring change. Railroads in the 1800s let towns grow quickly. Cars and highways later let people live farther from work.
People move for many reasons: jobs, family, safety or freedom. When new people arrive, they bring new foods, languages and traditions.
Historians study change using primary sources, made at the time, like letters and photos, and secondary sources, written later, like textbooks.
units.try: Find an old photo of your town or a nearby city, or ask an older neighbor. Compare it with today. List three things that changed and one that stayed the same.

learn: An immigrant is a person who moves to a new country to live. The United States has welcomed people from all over the world.
Between 1892 and 1954, about 12 million immigrants passed through Ellis Island in New York. Many others arrived at Angel Island in California.
Immigrants often faced hard times: new languages, low pay and sometimes unfair treatment.
Not everyone came by choice. Millions of Africans were captured and enslaved and brought here by force. Their strength and culture shaped our nation too.
units.try: Ask your family where your ancestors came from. Find those places on a world map. If your family is Native American, find your nation's homeland.
check: A person who moves to a new country to live
Where did many immigrants arrive in New York?

learn: Government has three levels: local, state and national (federal).
Local government runs cities and towns. It is often led by a mayor and a city council. It provides police, fire departments, parks, libraries and trash pickup.
State government is led by a governor. A state legislature makes state laws.
Governments pay for services with taxes, which is money that citizens and businesses pay.
units.try: Find out who your mayor and governor are. Then make a list of three services your city provides and how they help your family.
check: How do governments pay for services?

learn: Citizens have rights, which are freedoms they are promised. In the United States these include freedom of speech and freedom of religion.
Citizens also have responsibilities, which are duties. These include obeying laws, paying taxes, voting when old enough and serving on a jury.
The Constitution is the plan for our national government. The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments, or changes, to it.
People can work together to change laws peacefully: by voting, writing to leaders and speaking at public meetings.
units.try: Write a short letter to a local leader about something you would like to improve in your community, like a safer crosswalk or a cleaner park. Be polite and give a reason.
check: What is the Bill of Rights?
The first ten amendments to the Constitution
Which is a responsibility of citizens?

learn: People earn income by working. They use money to buy goods and services.
Because money is limited, people must make choices. The thing you give up when you choose is called the opportunity cost.
A budget is a plan for how to spend and save money. Saving helps you buy bigger things later or be ready for emergencies.
Banks keep money safe. Some savings accounts pay interest, which is extra money for keeping your money there.
units.try: Pretend you earn 10 dollars. Make a budget: decide how much to save, spend and share. If you choose a book over a toy, what is your opportunity cost?
check: What you give up when you choose
A plan for spending and saving

learn: Communities trade because no place can make everything it needs. Specialization means focusing on making what you do best.
Imports are goods brought into a country. Exports are goods sent out to other countries.
The United States exports goods like airplanes, corn and soybeans. It imports goods like coffee, bananas and many electronics.
Transportation by ship, train, truck and plane makes trade possible around the world.
units.try: Check the labels on five items at home, like clothes or toys. Write down where each was made. Find those countries on a world map.
check: A good brought into a country
A good sent out of a country
No place can make everything it needs

learn: Culture is the way of life of a group of people: their language, food, clothing, music, beliefs and traditions.
The United States has many cultures. People celebrate holidays such as Lunar New Year, Diwali, Hanukkah, Christmas, Eid and Kwanzaa.
National holidays honor our shared history. Independence Day, July 4, celebrates the Declaration of Independence in 1776. Martin Luther King Jr. Day honors his work for equal rights.
Learning about other cultures helps us understand and respect each other.
units.try: Interview a friend or neighbor about a holiday or tradition their family celebrates. Ask what they eat, wear and do. Share one new thing you learned.

rooms.about: This year we use the elements of art and principles of design, practice drawing, painting, collage, printmaking and sculpture, and learn about artists and art from many cultures.

learn: The elements of art are the building blocks artists use: line, shape, form, color, value, texture and space.

Line is a moving point. Shape is a flat closed area. Form has three dimensions. Color comes from light. Value is how light or dark something is. Texture is how it feels. Space is the area around and between things.
Every artwork uses several elements together.
Knowing these words helps you talk and write about art.
units.try: Look at any picture or painting in a book. Find and name at least four elements of art in it. For example: curved lines, a dark value, a rough texture.
check: How light or dark something is
Which is an element of art?

learn: Value shows light and dark. A value scale goes from white, through grays, to black.
Shading uses value to make flat shapes look 3D. A circle with shading on one side looks like a ball.
Find the light source. The side facing the light is lightest. The opposite side is darkest. Objects also cast a shadow on the ground.
Ways to shade: press harder with a pencil, hatch with parallel lines, cross-hatch with crossing lines, or use dots, called stippling.
units.try: Draw a value scale of five boxes from white to black using one pencil. Then draw a circle, pick a light source, and shade it to look like a ball with a shadow.
check: What makes a circle look like a ball?

learn: Complementary colors are opposite each other on the color wheel: red and green, blue and orange, yellow and violet. Side by side, they make each other look brighter.
Analogous colors sit next to each other on the wheel, like yellow, yellow-green and green. They look calm and connected.
Monochromatic art uses one color with its tints and shades.
Neutral colors are black, white, gray and brown. They can calm down bright colors.
units.try: Make two small paintings or drawings of the same fish. Use complementary colors for one and analogous colors for the other. Which one stands out more?
check: What is the complement of blue?
One color with its tints and shades

learn: Artists create the feeling of deep space on flat paper.
The foreground is closest to you, at the bottom of the page. The middle ground is in the middle. The background is farthest away, near the horizon line.
Objects in the background are drawn smaller, higher on the page and with less detail.
Faraway mountains often look lighter and bluer. This is called atmospheric perspective.
units.try: Draw a landscape with a horizon line. Put a big tree in the foreground, a house in the middle ground and small mountains in the background. Make the mountains light.
check: Smaller and higher on the page

learn: The principles of design are ways artists arrange the elements. They include balance, pattern, rhythm, emphasis, contrast, unity and movement.
Balance is how weight is spread. Symmetrical balance is the same on both sides, like a butterfly. Asymmetrical balance uses different things that still feel even.
Emphasis is the center of interest, the part your eye sees first. Contrast, like light against dark, can create emphasis.
Unity means all the parts feel like they belong together.
units.try: Fold a paper in half. Paint on one side, then fold and press to make a symmetrical print. Open it. What does it look like? Add one bright spot of color for emphasis.
check: The part your eye sees first

learn: A collage is art made by gluing pieces of paper, fabric, photos or other materials onto a surface.
Artists choose materials for their color, pattern and texture. Torn edges look soft. Cut edges look sharp.
Overlap pieces to make depth. Put background pieces down first.
Mixed media means using more than one material, like paint plus paper plus string.
units.try: Make a collage of a city or a forest using old magazines, wrapping paper and scraps. Tear some edges and cut others. Glue background pieces first, then the foreground.
check: Art made by gluing pieces onto a surface
What should you glue down first?

learn: A portrait is a picture of a person. A self-portrait is a picture of yourself.
Faces follow proportions. The eyes are about halfway down the head, not at the top. The bottom of the nose is about halfway between the eyes and the chin.
The mouth sits about one-third of the way from the nose to the chin. The tops of the ears line up with the eyes.
Artists show personality through expression, clothing and background.
units.try: Look in a mirror and draw a self-portrait. Lightly draw an oval, then a line halfway down for the eyes. Place the nose and mouth using the proportions you learned.
check: Where are the eyes on a face?

learn: Relief printing uses a raised surface. Ink touches only the raised parts, which print onto paper.
In foam printing, you press lines into a foam sheet with a dull pencil. The pressed lines stay white when printed.
Prints come out reversed, like a mirror. Letters must be carved backward to read correctly.
An edition is a set of matching prints. Artists number them, like 1/5, 2/5.
units.try: Press a simple design into a clean foam tray with a dull pencil. Roll or brush paint over it, then press paper on top and rub gently. Peel it off. Is your design reversed?
check: In relief printing, which parts get ink?

learn: Clay can be shaped by pinching, coiling and slab building.
Coils are long ropes of clay stacked into walls. Slabs are flat sheets of clay cut and joined.
To join clay pieces, score them by scratching both surfaces, add slip (a mix of clay and water), and press them together.
Clay must dry slowly. Then it is fired in a very hot oven called a kiln to become hard.
units.try: Use clay or play dough to build a small coil pot. Roll five ropes, make a flat base, and stack the coils around it. Smooth the inside with your finger.
check: How do you join two pieces of clay?
A very hot oven for clay

learn: Artists get ideas from their lives and cultures.
Georgia O'Keeffe painted huge close-up flowers and the deserts of New Mexico. Jacob Lawrence painted bold series that told the story of Black families moving north.
Aboriginal artists of Australia have used dot patterns and symbols to tell stories about land and ancestors.
Studying art from many places shows how people share ideas, beliefs and history.
units.try: Choose an object from nature, like a flower or a shell. Draw it very large and close up, so it fills the whole page, like O'Keeffe's flowers.
check: What did Georgia O'Keeffe often paint?
What do Aboriginal dot paintings often tell?

rooms.about: This year we read rhythms and notes on the staff, learn meter and dynamics, explore the orchestra, sing in rounds, and listen to music from many times and places.

learn: Beats are grouped into sets. This is called meter. Music in 2 feels like a march. Music in 3 feels like a waltz. Music in 4 is very common.
Bar lines divide music into measures. Each measure has the same number of beats.
A time signature tells the beats in each measure. In 4/4 time, the top 4 means four beats per measure.
The first beat of each measure is often the strongest. It is called the downbeat.
units.try: Count out loud 1-2-3, 1-2-3 and clap only on beat 1. That is 3/4 time, the waltz feel. Then try 1-2-3-4 with a clap on 1. Which feels like marching?
check: In 3/4 time, how many beats are in a measure?

learn: Notes have different lengths. A whole note lasts 4 beats. A half note lasts 2 beats. A quarter note lasts 1 beat. Two eighth notes together last 1 beat.
Sixteenth notes are even faster. Four sixteenth notes fit in one beat.
Each note has a matching rest of the same length: whole rest, half rest, quarter rest.
A dot after a note adds half its value. A dotted half note lasts 2 + 1 = 3 beats.
units.try: Clap and count: quarter, quarter, half note (hold 2 beats). Then: half, half. Then: whole note (hold 4 beats). Each line should take four beats.
check: How many beats does a half note get?
How long is a dotted half note?

learn: Music is written on a staff of five lines and four spaces. Notes higher on the staff sound higher.
The treble clef is used for higher sounds. It is also called the G clef because it curls around the G line.
The lines of the treble staff, from bottom to top, are E, G, B, D, F. A saying to remember: Every Good Boy Does Fine.
The spaces, from bottom to top, spell FACE. Music uses only the letters A to G, then starts over.
units.try: Draw a staff with five lines. Write the letters E, G, B, D, F on the lines and F, A, C, E in the spaces. Then spell words with notes, like BAG, CAGE or FACE.
check: What do the treble spaces spell?
How many lines does a staff have?

learn: A scale is a set of notes going up or down in order. The C major scale is C, D, E, F, G, A, B, C.
Singers often use solfège: do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do.
A melody moves by steps (next-door notes) or skips and leaps (jumping over notes).
Melodies often end on do, the home note. It sounds finished.
units.try: Sing do, re, mi, fa, so, la, ti, do going up, then back down. Then sing a short song and notice whether the melody moves by steps or leaps.
check: What is the home note in solfège?
What is a step in a melody?

learn: Dynamics are music's loud and soft. From softest to loudest: pianissimo (pp), piano (p), mezzo piano (mp), mezzo forte (mf), forte (f), fortissimo (ff).
Mezzo means medium. Mezzo forte means medium loud.
Tempo is speed. Largo is very slow, andante is a walking pace, allegro is fast and presto is very fast.
Ritardando means gradually slow down. Accelerando means gradually speed up. Most of these terms come from Italian.
units.try: Sing a favorite song four ways: pianissimo, fortissimo, largo and presto. Which way fits the song best? Why?
check: Which tempo is a walking pace?

learn: A round is a song where groups sing the same melody but start at different times. The parts overlap and fit together.
When different notes sound at the same time, that is harmony.
An ostinato is a short pattern that repeats over and over. It can be a rhythm or a melody under the main song.
Singing in parts takes careful listening. Keep your part steady while hearing the others.
units.try: With family, sing a simple round like a rowing song you know. One person starts; the next starts when the first reaches the second line. Keep going and listen to the harmony.
check: The same melody started at different times

learn: An orchestra is a large group of instruments with four families: strings, woodwinds, brass and percussion.
The strings are the largest family. From highest to lowest: violin, viola, cello and double bass.
The conductor leads the orchestra, keeping the tempo and showing when to play louder or softer.
Larger instruments usually make lower sounds. A tuba plays lower than a trumpet.
units.try: Listen to a piece of orchestra music. Pretend to be the conductor. Move your arm to the beat. Try to name one instrument family you hear.
check: Which string instrument plays the lowest?

learn: Form is the plan of a piece of music. Letters name the sections.
In rondo form, the A section keeps coming back between new sections: A B A C A.
Theme and variations starts with a melody (the theme) and then changes it in different ways: faster, slower, in a new key or with new instruments.
Listening for repeated sections helps you understand and remember music.
units.try: Create a rondo with body percussion. A: clap clap stomp. B: pat your knees four times. C: snap four times. Perform A B A C A.
check: In theme and variations, what happens to the theme?
It is changed in different ways

learn: Composers write music. Music has changed over hundreds of years.
Johann Sebastian Bach (1685 to 1750) wrote music with many melodies woven together. Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart (1756 to 1791) began composing as a young child.
Ludwig van Beethoven (1770 to 1827) kept composing even after he became deaf.
In America, Scott Joplin was famous for ragtime piano music, and Duke Ellington led a great jazz orchestra.
units.try: Pick one composer from this unit. Listen to a short piece by them with a grown-up. Draw what the music makes you imagine and describe its tempo and dynamics.
check: Which composer kept writing music after becoming deaf?
What style of music is Scott Joplin famous for?

learn: Music is part of every culture. It is used for celebrations, work, worship, storytelling and dance.
Steel pans from Trinidad and Tobago were first made from oil drums. The gamelan of Indonesia is a group of bronze gongs and metal instruments.
Folk songs are passed down by people singing them. Work songs helped people keep rhythm during hard labor.
Spirituals were created by enslaved Black people in America. They expressed sorrow, faith and hope for freedom.
units.try: Ask a family member about a song from their childhood or culture. Learn to sing part of it. Tell where it comes from and when people sang it.
check: What were the first steel pans made from?

rooms.about: This year we build fitness and sports skills, learn how our bodies work, and practice healthy choices about food, hygiene, safety, feelings and friendships.

learn: Physical fitness has parts. Heart and lung endurance means your heart and lungs can work for a long time, like when you run or swim.
Muscle strength is how much force a muscle can make. Muscle endurance is how long a muscle can keep working.
Flexibility is how far your joints can move. Stretching helps.
Kids need at least 60 minutes of activity a day, with hard activities on at least 3 days a week.
units.try: Do a fitness check: jog in place 1 minute (endurance), do as many wall push-ups as you can (strength), and reach toward your toes for 15 seconds (flexibility). Write down your results to compare later.
check: How far your joints can move
How many minutes of activity do kids need each day?

learn: Your heart pumps blood that carries oxygen to your body. At rest, a kid's heart beats about 70 to 110 times a minute.
Your lungs breathe in air. Oxygen moves from your lungs into your blood.
Your body has more than 600 muscles. Muscles pull on bones to move you. Bones and muscles work together.
Exercise makes the heart, lungs and muscles stronger over time.
units.try: Count your heartbeats for 15 seconds while resting and multiply by 4. Then do 1 minute of jumping jacks and count again. How much did it rise?
check: What does blood carry to the body?

learn: Dribbling means moving a ball while controlling it. In basketball, dribble with your fingertips, not your palm.
Keep the ball at about waist height and to the side. Try to look up, not at the ball.
In soccer, dribble with gentle taps using the inside and outside of your foot.
To kick for distance, place your non-kicking foot beside the ball and kick with your shoelaces.
units.try: With a ball outside, dribble with your hand 20 times without losing control. Then dribble a ball with your feet around three objects and back. Count how long it takes.
check: What part of your hand should you dribble with?
Where does your non-kicking foot go?

learn: Striking means hitting an object with your hand or a tool, like a paddle or bat.
Keep your eyes on the object. Step toward your target as you swing.
Volleying means hitting a ball in the air before it touches the ground, like in volleyball.
Use a flat hand or forearms, and keep your body under the ball.
units.try: Keep a balloon in the air using only your hands. Count how many taps you can do in a row. Then try only your forearms.
check: What should you watch when striking?
Hitting a ball before it lands

learn: Good teammates encourage each other, share the ball and include everyone.
Good sportsmanship means playing fairly, following rules and being kind whether you win or lose.
Say good game to the other team. Do not brag or blame others.
Disagreements happen. Stay calm, listen and look for a fair solution.
units.try: Play a simple game with family, like tag or catch. Practice saying one encouraging thing to each player and good game at the end.
check: Being kind whether you win or lose
What should you say after a game?

learn: Nutrients in food give your body energy and help it grow. Carbohydrates give energy. Proteins build muscles. Fats store energy. Vitamins, minerals and water keep your body working.
A balanced plate has fruits, vegetables, grains, protein and dairy. Choose whole grains, like brown rice and whole wheat bread, more often.
Read food labels. They tell serving size, calories, sugar and more.
Eat breakfast. It gives your brain energy to learn.
units.try: Plan a healthy breakfast that includes at least three food groups. Draw it on a paper plate and label each food's group.
check: What does a food label tell you?

learn: Germs like bacteria and viruses can spread by touching, coughing and sneezing.
Wash hands with soap for at least 20 seconds, especially before eating and after the bathroom.
Brush teeth twice a day for two minutes and floss once a day. Sugary foods help bacteria make holes in teeth called cavities.
Bathe regularly, wear clean clothes and get 9 to 12 hours of sleep each night.
units.try: Make a hygiene checklist for one week: brushing morning and night, flossing, washing hands, and bedtime. Check each box when done.
check: Bacteria using sugar to make holes in teeth
How much sleep do kids your age need?

learn: Fire safety: if there is a fire, get out and stay out. Crawl low under smoke. Feel doors with the back of your hand; if hot, use another way out.
If your clothes catch fire: stop, drop and roll.
Never touch medicine, cleaning products or weapons. If you find one, do not touch it; tell an adult right away.
Water safety: swim only with an adult watching. Wear a life jacket on boats.
units.try: With your family, draw a fire escape map of your home. Show two ways out of each room and a meeting spot outside. Practice it once.
check: What should you do if your clothes catch fire?
What should you do if you find a weapon?
Don't touch it and tell an adult

learn: Feelings are natural. Naming them helps you understand them: I feel frustrated, worried or proud.
Stress is how your body reacts to a challenge. A little helps you focus. Too much can cause headaches, stomachaches or trouble sleeping.
Healthy ways to cope include deep breathing, talking to someone you trust, exercising, drawing or taking a break.
Trusted adults include parents, teachers, school counselors and doctors.
units.try: Make a calm-down card. Write five things that help you feel better, like breathing slowly, hugging a pet or going for a walk. Keep it somewhere you can see.
check: Which is a healthy way to cope with stress?

learn: Healthy friends are kind, honest, fair and respectful. They listen and take turns.
Bullying is when someone hurts another person on purpose, again and again. It can be hitting, mean words, leaving people out or spreading rumors, including online.
If you are bullied, tell the person to stop in a firm voice, walk away and tell a trusted adult.
If you see bullying, be an upstander. Stand with the person, help them get away and tell an adult.
units.try: Practice with a family member. Say in a firm, calm voice, Stop. I don't like that. Then practice walking away and telling an adult what happened.
check: Someone who helps when they see bullying
Which is a sign of a healthy friend?
